verdict.reasoning: Patient states: "I've been having, uh, diarrhoea, for like, let's say past three days, more or less."
Frequency: "around, five to six times a day"; consistency: "it's definitely, definitely watery, uh, loose stools".
Patient says: "it started with vomiting, so I vomited a couple of times"; the exact number of two episodes is not stated, only "a couple of times" which is approximate.
Doctor: "the vomiting has now stopped. Is that right?" Patient: "Yes, yes."
Doctor: "Any blood in your stools?" Patient: "No, not that I could see."
Doctor: "with the diarrhea have you noticed any other symptoms, like tummy pain?" Patient: "Uh, not, not really, no."
Patient: "I feel like I don't drink enough... and I feel dehydrated again" and earlier "I feel very dehydrated."
Doctor: "have you managed to eat anything, solids?" Patient: "Uh, not much, not much. So just a little bit."
Patient: "I don't really feel like, uh, I have appetite."
Doctor: "Have you had any other symptoms, like fever or temperature?" Patient: "probably at, at the beginning I was feeling I had a bit of temperature."
Patient: "but now I feel, I feel kind of fine" after describing initial feeling of temperature; implies currently not feverish.
Patient: "I feel very weak though."
Doctor: "Any headaches or muscle pains?" Patient: "Not, not really, no." This includes denial of headache.
Same exchange: "Any headaches or muscle pains?" Patient: "Not, not really, no." Denies myalgias (muscle pains).
Food trigger queried: "Did you have any takeaway food, or any dodgy restaurant food?" Patient: "Uh, not that I remember, no." Indicates no known food trigger.
Doctor: "Have you been around anyone unwell, with diarrhea recently, last week or so?" Patient: "Hmm, not that I know, not that I." This is a denial of sick contacts.
Patient: "I do suffer of asthma. So, I do have my inhalers."
Patient: "I do have my inhalers... I use infrequently"; Doctor clarifies: "Is that the blue inhaler?" Patient confirms. A blue inhaler used infrequently implies a PRN short-acting beta-agonist.
Doctor: "Do you have any allergies to medications?" Patient: "Um, not that I know of."
Patient: "my father has, high uh, well used to have high blood pressure."
Patient: "He actually, so he actually died, of, bowel cancer, like ten years ago."
Patient: "my mother... she has diabetes." Doctor: "Do you know if that's type one or type two?" Patient: "Uh, it's type two."
Doctor: "Who lives at home with you, sir?" Patient: "Ohh I, I live alone."
Doctor: "What's your employment? What do you do for work?" Patient: "I'm a software engineer."
Patient: "these last three days I've been feeling, really unwell, so I couldn't work."
Doctor: "regarding your smoking and alcohol. Do you do either of those?" Patient: "I... drink infrequently, like socially let's say, and I don't smoke."
Same quote: "I drink infrequently, like socially let's say."

Doctor: "you're probably suffering from what we call gastroenteritis" and patient repeatedly reports feeling very dehydrated; this supports assessment of acute gastroenteritis with dehydration symptoms.
Doctor: "you can drink plenty of fluids. Really try and flush the toxins out of your body."
Doctor: "you can get things from the pharmacy, which is called Dioralyte... it's a type of fluid replacement drink."
Doctor: "you can take some Paracetamol if you're feeling feverish and weak."
Doctor: "I would probably advise you to continue taking time off work for next day or two, until you get better."
Doctor: "normally you have to be diarrhea-free for about  to  hours, before you return back to work." Although the exact hours are unclear, the instruction to return once diarrhea-free is given.
Doctor: "If you're still not better next week, I want you to come back and see me. And we can have another look at your symptoms, OK?"
